folder: Principles of Diagnostic Medicine I Exam 2

items.section_title: 9.3 · Objective c — Indications for ordering a lipid profile
items.html: Apolipoprotein B monitoring. It is a modifiable, treatment-responsive marker, so it is used repeatedly to guide and monitor lipid-lowering therapy, unlike lipoprotein(a), which is fixed and measured once.

src.question: A 62-year-old on lipid-lowering therapy is followed with repeated apoB (apolipoprotein B) levels. Why is apoB suited to that role?
src.key: It is modifiable and responds to treatment
src.explanation: ApoB is a modifiable, treatment-responsive marker used repeatedly to guide and monitor lipid-lowering therapy, unlike lipoprotein(a), which is fixed and measured once.

items.section_title: 9.4 · Objective d — Analyzing a lipid profile
items.html: Non-HDL-C. It equals total cholesterol minus HDL-C (210 minus 50 is 160 mg/dL), is followed against a risk-based goal, and needs no triglyceride value and costs nothing extra.

src.question: A 50-year-old's panel shows total cholesterol 210 mg/dL and HDL-C (high-density lipoprotein cholesterol) 50 mg/dL. What is the non-HDL-C, the value followed against a risk-based goal?
src.key: 160 mg/dL
src.explanation: Non-HDL-C is total cholesterol minus HDL-C: 210 minus 50 is 160 mg/dL. It needs no triglyceride value and costs nothing extra.

items.section_title: 9.5 · Objective e — Lipid testing in cardiovascular risk assessment
items.html: Fasting for a lipid profile. Nonfasting samples are acceptable for most people. Fasting is reserved for triglycerides of 400 mg/dL or above, triglyceride disorders, or a family history of premature disease or genetic dyslipidemia.

src.question: A 40-year-old with no risk factors is due a routine lipid profile and has eaten breakfast. Is the sample acceptable?
src.key: Yes, nonfasting is acceptable for most
src.explanation: Nonfasting is acceptable for most people. Fasting is reserved for triglycerides of 400 mg/dL or above, triglyceride disorders, or a family history of premature disease or genetic dyslipidemia.

items.section_title: 9.2 · Objective b — Indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
items.html: Troponin beyond first diagnosis. Troponins also detect reocclusion and reinfarction, and procedure-related infarction, such as returning chest pain after a stent.

src.question: A 65-year-old had a stent placed yesterday and his chest pain has returned. Which use of troponin applies?
src.key: Detecting reinfarction
src.explanation: Troponins detect reocclusion and reinfarction, and procedure-related infarction, among their applications beyond the first diagnosis.

items.section_title: 9.6 · Objective f — Lipids and lipoproteins in atherosclerosis
items.html: Lipoprotein(a) testing. The level is more than 90% genetically determined, so testing is indicated with a personal or family history of atherosclerotic disease and extends to first-degree relatives through cascade testing in appropriate families.

src.question: A 41-year-old man is found to have a markedly elevated lipoprotein(a) after a premature myocardial infarction. Whom should testing be extended to?
src.key: His first-degree relatives
src.explanation: Testing is indicated in those with a personal or family history of atherosclerotic disease, with cascade testing in appropriate families, because the level is more than 90% genetically determined.

items.section_title: 8.5 · Objective f.i — Echocardiography
items.html: Transthoracic echocardiography. It is the most common echo procedure because it can be performed at the bedside and is noninvasive. Availability, not image quality, makes it the default, and the trade is detail at the back of the heart.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: Why is transthoracic echocardiography the most common echo procedure?
src.key: It can be performed at the bedside and is noninvasive
src.explanation: Availability rather than image quality is what makes it the default, and the trade is detail at the back of the heart.

items.section_title: 8.6 · Objective f.ii — Stress testing
items.html: Echocardiographic stress test. It is the appropriate initial choice for a patient who can exercise but whose resting tracing is abnormal, since the electrocardiogram cannot be read for ischemia if already abnormal and imaging must carry the answer.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 37

src.question: For which patient is an echocardiographic stress test the appropriate initial choice?
src.key: One who can exercise but whose resting tracing is abnormal
src.explanation: The electrocardiogram cannot be read for ischemia if it is already abnormal, so the imaging has to carry the answer instead.

items.section_title: 8.5 · Objective f.i — Echocardiography
items.html: Transesophageal echocardiography. Unlike the transthoracic study, it requires throat anesthesia, sedation and monitoring. It is a procedure rather than a scan, so it carries a contraindication list.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 25

src.question: What does a transesophageal study require that a transthoracic one does not?
src.key: Throat anesthesia, sedation and monitoring
src.explanation: It is a procedure rather than a scan, which is why it carries a contraindication list and the transthoracic study does not.

items.section_title: 8.8 · Objective f.iv — Cardiac CT (computed tomography) and CT angiography
items.html: Cardiac computed tomography preparation. Cardiac medications are given to control heart rate, since the moving heart degrades the images. The study is also synchronized to an electrocardiogram so the heart can be examined at chosen points in the cycle.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 41

src.question: Why are cardiac medications given before a cardiac computed tomography study?
src.key: To control heart rate, since the moving heart degrades the images
src.explanation: and the study is also synchronized to an electrocardiogram so the heart can be examined at chosen points in the cycle.

items.section_title: 8.6 · Objective f.ii — Stress testing
items.html: Post-exercise echocardiogram. It looks for abnormal left ventricular wall motion induced by exercise. The finding is transient and resolves as the heart recovers, so the patient dismounts quickly and is imaged promptly.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 37

src.question: What is the echocardiogram looking for after exercise, and why must it be obtained quickly?
src.key: Abnormal left ventricular wall motion induced by exercise
src.explanation: The finding is transient, so the patient is asked to dismount quickly and the heart is imaged before it settles. Which resolves as the heart recovers.

items.section_title: 8.8 · Objective f.iv — Cardiac CT (computed tomography) and CT angiography
items.html: Blooming artifact. Heavy calcification appears larger than it is on cardiac computed tomography, so a stenosis looks more severe; it exaggerates the very lesion the study was ordered to assess.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: What is the blooming artifact, and why does it matter?
src.key: Heavy calcification appears larger than it is
src.explanation: The artifact exaggerates the very lesion the study was ordered to assess, which is a limitation worth naming rather than a curiosity. So a stenosis looks more severe.

items.section_title: 8.8 · Objective f.iv — Cardiac CT (computed tomography) and CT angiography
items.html: Cardiac computed tomography indications. Pre-operative planning before cardiac surgery, particularly valvular and great vessel procedures, is an indication, alongside calcium deposits, coronary anatomical anomalies and congenital disease. It is usually done immediately before the angiographic study.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: Which is an indication for cardiac computed tomography rather than the angiographic study?
src.key: Pre-operative planning before cardiac surgery
src.explanation: alongside calcium deposits, coronary anatomical anomalies and congenital disease, and it is usually done immediately before the angiographic study. Particularly valvular and great vessel procedures.

items.section_title: 8.7 · Objective f.iii — Nuclear cardiology
items.html: Nuclear stress pattern. Tracer uptake that is normal at rest but reduced after stress indicates inducible ischemia from a coronary stenosis: the tissue is alive but cannot increase its supply when demand rises.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 48

src.question: Tracer uptake in a region is normal at rest but reduced after stress. What does that pattern indicate?
src.key: Inducible ischemia, from a coronary stenosis
src.explanation: The tissue is alive but cannot increase its supply when demand rises, which is what a stenosis does.

items.section_title: 8.2 · Objective c — Common abnormal findings
items.html: Vascular ultrasound appearance. The denser the structure, the lighter it appears, so air is black and bone is near white. Superficial structures sit nearer the top of the screen.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 14

src.question: On a vascular ultrasound, how does tissue density relate to the image?
src.key: The denser the structure the lighter it appears
src.explanation: and superficial structures sit nearer the top of the screen, which together let you orient any image without being told what it is. So air is black and bone is near white.

items.section_title: 8.10 · Objective f.vi — Coronary angiography and the invasive studies
items.html: Catheter ablation. During electrophysiological testing it inactivates part of the heart by destroying that tissue, not merely silencing it, which makes the treatment definitive.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 62

src.question: What does catheter ablation do during electrophysiological testing?
src.key: Inactivates part of the heart by destroying that tissue
src.explanation: The tissue is not merely silenced but destroyed, which is what makes the treatment definitive.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Objectives g & h — Waves, segments, intervals and their normal values
items.html: Corrected QT above 500 milliseconds. A corrected QT beyond five hundred milliseconds is high risk prolongation, above the borderline range that begins in the low four hundreds.

src.question: A corrected QT of 520 milliseconds is reported. How should that be read?
src.key: High risk prolongation
src.explanation: Beyond five hundred milliseconds is the high risk band, above the borderline range that begins in the low four hundreds.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Objectives g & h — Waves, segments, intervals and their normal values
items.html: Corrected QT. It is used rather than the raw QT interval because the QT interval changes with heart rate; without correcting, the same heart would show different values at different rates.

src.question: Why is the corrected QT used rather than the raw QT interval?
src.key: The QT interval changes with heart rate
src.explanation: Without correcting, the same heart would appear to have a different QT at different rates. The correction accounts for it.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Objectives g & h — Waves, segments, intervals and their normal values
items.html: Q wave. It represents depolarization of the interventricular septum, which travels away from lead II and so gives a downward deflection. It is not always visible.

src.question: What does the Q wave represent, and why is it negative in lead II?
src.key: Depolarization of the interventricular septum, which travels away from lead II
src.explanation: The direction of that particular wavefront is what makes the deflection downward, and it is not always visible.

items.section_title: 7.1 · Objective a — The action potential and the conduction system
items.html: Relative refractory period. Unlike the absolute period, a sufficiently strong stimulus can produce a response. The cell is excitable but not fully recovered, so a stimulus arriving then can start something abnormal.

src.question: What distinguishes the relative from the absolute refractory period?
src.key: In the relative period a sufficiently strong stimulus can produce a response
src.explanation: It is the dangerous window: the cell is excitable again but not yet fully recovered, so a stimulus arriving there can start something abnormal.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Objectives g & h — Waves, segments, intervals and their normal values
items.html: ST segment. It falls between ventricular depolarization and repolarization, when the ventricles hold their contraction to allow emptying; it is the part of the beat that does the ejecting.

src.question: What is happening mechanically during the ST segment?
src.key: The ventricles are holding their contraction to allow emptying
src.explanation: It falls between ventricular depolarization and repolarization, and it is the part of the beat that does the ejecting.

items.section_title: 7.6 · Objective f — Determining heart rate
items.html: Six-second rate method. Multiply the QRS count in a six-second strip by ten, since six seconds is a tenth of a minute; eight complexes give a ventricular rate of eighty beats per minute.

src.question: A six-second strip contains eight QRS complexes. What is the ventricular rate?
src.key: Eighty beats per minute
src.explanation: The six-second method multiplies the count by ten, since six seconds is a tenth of a minute.

items.section_title: 9.1 · Objective a — Creatine kinase, troponins, BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) and hs-CRP (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein)
items.html: Troponin subunits. Troponin I, the inhibitory component, has cardiac specificity; troponin T is primarily cardiac, but trace amounts are detected in skeletal muscle.

src.question: A 59-year-old's troponin is being interpreted. Which troponin subunit has cardiac specificity?
src.key: Troponin I, the inhibitory component
src.explanation: Troponin I has cardiac specificity. Troponin T is primarily cardiac, but trace amounts are detected in skeletal muscle.

items.section_title: 9.6 · Objective f — Lipids and lipoproteins in atherosclerosis
items.html: Lipoprotein(a) measurement. It generally needs measuring once in a lifetime: it is more than 90% genetically determined and stable over life, and needs no fasting.

src.question: A 35-year-old has lipoprotein(a) measured for the first time. How often does it generally need measuring?
src.key: Once in a lifetime
src.explanation: It is more than 90% genetically determined and stable over life, and needs no fasting, so a single measurement generally suffices.

items.section_title: 9.1 · Objective a — Creatine kinase, troponins, BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) and hs-CRP (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein)
items.html: Troponin versus CK-MB. Troponin is preferred because it rises sooner and stays elevated longer, expanding the window for diagnosis and treatment, which matters for a patient presenting late.

src.question: A 55-year-old presents two days after an episode of chest pain. Why is troponin preferred over CK-MB (creatine kinase muscle-brain isoenzyme)?
src.key: It rises sooner and stays elevated longer
src.explanation: That expands the window for diagnosis and treatment, which matters for a patient presenting late.

items.section_title: 8.5 · Objective f.i — Echocardiography
items.html: Contraindications to a transesophageal study besides esophageal disease. An uncooperative patient or altered mental status, restricted neck movement (cervical spine arthritis with reduced range of motion), and airway risk (obstructive sleep apnea or other risk of airway compromise).
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: Which patient factors, other than esophageal disease, contraindicate a transesophageal study?
src.key: An uncooperative patient, restricted neck movement, airway risk
src.explanation: Two are about whether the patient can be positioned and kept still, and one is about whether the airway can be protected under sedation. In full: altered mental status or an uncooperative patient, cervical spine arthritis with reduced range of motion, and obstructive sleep apnea or other risk of airway compromise.

items.section_title: 8.1 · Objectives a & b — Cardiovascular anatomy and the cardiac silhouette
items.html: Chest radiography in cardiac evaluation. It is not the primary modality, but it gives useful clues when obtained; it is frequently the study already in hand, so reading it well matters.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 4

src.question: What is the standing of chest radiography in cardiac evaluation?
src.key: It is not the primary modality, but it gives useful clues when obtained
src.explanation: It is rarely the study you order to answer a cardiac question, and frequently the study you already have, which is why reading it well matters.

items.section_title: 8.5 · Objective f.i — Echocardiography
items.html: Transesophageal study in cerebral ischemia. It can find thrombus in the left atrial appendage, looking for the source rather than the consequence; the appendage is the site the transthoracic study sees worst.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 23

src.question: Why is a transesophageal study used in a patient presenting with cerebral ischemia?
src.key: It can find thrombus in the left atrial appendage
src.explanation: It looks for the source rather than the consequence, and the appendage is the site the transthoracic study sees worst.

items.section_title: 8.10 · Objective f.vi — Coronary angiography and the invasive studies
items.html: Coronary angiography. It is performed under local anesthesia with intravenous sedation, with catheters guided by fluoroscopy and contrast injected into each coronary artery; pressures are measured as the catheter goes, giving hemodynamic information alongside the pictures.
cites: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 72

src.question: How is coronary angiography performed?
src.key: Under local anesthesia with intravenous sedation
src.explanation: and pressures are measured as the catheter goes, so it yields hemodynamic information alongside the pictures. With catheters guided by fluoroscopy and contrast injected into each coronary artery.

items.section_title: 7.5 · Objective e — Limb and precordial leads and their placement
items.html: Contiguous leads. These are two or more leads looking at the same area of the heart, so a change in a contiguous group means more than the same change in one isolated lead.

src.question: What are contiguous leads?
src.key: Two or more leads looking at the same area of the heart
src.explanation: which is why a change appearing in a contiguous group means more than the same change in one isolated lead.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Objectives g & h — Waves, segments, intervals and their normal values
items.html: S wave. A deflection must extend below the baseline to count as a true S wave; if it does not, it is called an S wave pattern instead.

src.question: What must a deflection do to count as a true S wave?
src.key: Extend below the baseline
src.explanation: If it does not, it is called an S wave pattern instead, which is a distinction of naming that matters when describing a tracing precisely.

items.section_title: 7.1 · Objective a — The action potential and the conduction system
items.html: Right bundle branch. It is much longer than the left, despite the left ventricle being the larger chamber; the anatomy does not follow chamber size.

src.question: What is noted about the length of the right bundle branch?
src.key: It is much longer than the left, despite the left ventricle being the larger chamber
src.explanation: and the counterintuitiveness is the point: the anatomy does not follow chamber size.

items.section_title: 7.1 · Objective a — The action potential and the conduction system
items.html: Phase 3, rapid repolarization. Calcium channels close while potassium channels remain open, returning the cell to minus ninety millivolts; the inward current stops and the outward one continues unopposed.

src.question: What happens during phase 3, rapid repolarization?
src.key: Calcium channels close while potassium channels remain open, returning the cell to minus ninety millivolts
src.explanation: The inward current stops and the outward one continues unopposed, which is why this phase is the rapid one.

items.section_title: 7.6 · Objective f — Determining heart rate
items.html: Regularity of the rhythm. When not obvious by eye, determine it by comparing consecutive R to R intervals with calipers, or with a marked sheet of paper.

src.question: How is regularity determined when it is not obvious by eye?
src.key: By comparing consecutive R to R intervals with calipers
src.explanation: The marked paper is the field substitute, and it answers the same question the calipers do. Or a marked sheet of paper.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Objectives g & h — Waves, segments, intervals and their normal values
items.html: Prominent U waves. They are associated with hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, prolonged QT and the period after myocardial infarction; the electrolyte associations are the practically useful ones.

src.question: Prominent U waves are associated with which conditions?
src.key: Hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, prolonged QT and the period after myocardial infarction
src.explanation: and the electrolyte associations are the practically useful ones, since the wave itself is not fully understood.

items.section_title: 7.5 · Objective e — Limb and precordial leads and their placement
items.html: Hexaxial reference system. It is used to determine the normal axis of the heart; six views in one plane make an axis calculable.

src.question: What is the hexaxial reference system used to determine?
src.key: The normal axis of the heart
src.explanation: Six views in one plane are what make an axis calculable at all.
